title: Design an Online Judge (LeetCode)
summary: End-to-end walkthrough: judge untrusted code in layered sandboxes, batch tests per submission behind a queue, survive contest bursts and serve a live Redis leaderboard.
body:
## Practice first

Design an online judge like LeetCode or Codeforces. Users browse coding problems, submit solutions in several languages, and get a verdict (accepted, wrong answer, time limit exceeded and so on) after the code runs against hidden test cases. The platform also hosts timed contests with a live leaderboard.

Spend about 10 minutes sketching first: requirements, the submission lifecycle from "Submit" to verdict, how you run untrusted code safely, and what happens at the exact moment a 50,000-person contest starts. Then compare with the walkthrough. The heart of this problem is that you are executing arbitrary code written by strangers, at bursty scale, and must return a fair verdict quickly.

## Functional requirements

Core (users should be able to):

1. **View problems:** list and read problem statements with examples.
2. **Submit code and get results:** submit a solution in a supported language and see the verdict, including per-test outcome summary, runtime and memory.
3. **Compete in contests:** join a timed contest and see a live leaderboard with their own rank.

Out of scope: authentication internals, discussion forums, editorials, plagiarism detection, the "Run with custom input" playground (it reuses the same execution path), and problem authoring tools.

## Non-functional requirements

- **Security and isolation (the top priority):** user code must not escape its sandbox, read hidden test data or other users' code, reach the network, or degrade other submissions. This is non-negotiable and shapes the whole execution tier.
- **Latency:** verdict for a typical submission within about 5 s at p50 and 15 s at p99 outside contests; during contest peaks, queueing may stretch this but must stay visible to users (they see "queued, position N").
- **Scale:** about 1 million submissions/day normally; contests of up to 50,000 participants with sharp bursts.
- **Durability and consistency, per operation:** an accepted submission is never lost (it is written durably before we return), and each logical submission is judged once in effect. Verdicts are strongly consistent for the submitter. The leaderboard can lag by a few seconds (eventual consistency is fine), but the final standings must be exact.
- **Fairness:** the same code on the same test should get the same verdict; time limits must not depend on how busy the host is.

## Back-of-the-envelope

- **Normal load:** 10^6 / 86,400 ≈ **12 submissions/s**.
- **Contest burst:** assume a quarter of 50,000 participants submit the easiest problem within the same 2 minutes: 12,500 / 120 ≈ **100 submissions/s**, with spikes to 200/s including resubmissions. That is **15 to 20 times normal load**, arriving within minutes, faster than reactive autoscaling of VMs can respond. **Decision:** pre-scale the worker pool before scheduled contests and absorb the rest with a queue.
- **CPU per submission:** compile 1 to 2 s for C++ or Java, plus 40 tests × about 50 ms ≈ 2 s of execution; call it 3 core-seconds. 200/s × 3 ≈ **600 cores** at contest peak, versus about 40 normally.
- **Sandbox startup cost:** starting a fresh container costs roughly 0.3 to 1 s. One sandbox per test would add 40 × 0.5 s = 20 s of overhead per submission, more than the code's own runtime. **Decision:** run all tests of a submission inside one sandbox.
- **Status polling:** 50,000 contestants polling every second is 50,000 reads/s of tiny status rows. **Decision:** serve status from a cache or push it over SSE, not from the primary database.

## Core entities

- **Problem:** ID, statement, limits (time per test, memory), supported languages, test set version.
- **Test case:** problem ID, ordinal, input and expected output (stored in object storage, never exposed).
- **Submission:** ID, user, problem, language, code reference, idempotency key, status, verdict, runtime, memory, failing test ordinal, contest ID (optional).
- **Contest:** ID, start and end, problem list, scoring rules, freeze time.
- **Contest standing:** contest, user, solved count, penalty, per-problem attempts and first-accepted time.

```mermaid
erDiagram
    PROBLEM ||--o{ TEST_CASE : has
    PROBLEM ||--o{ SUBMISSION : receives
    USER ||--o{ SUBMISSION : makes
    CONTEST ||--o{ PROBLEM : includes
    CONTEST ||--o{ STANDING : ranks
    USER ||--o{ STANDING : holds
    SUBMISSION {
        string id
        string idempotency_key
        string language
        string status
        string verdict
        int runtime_ms
    }
    STANDING {
        int solved
        int penalty_seconds
    }
```

Submissions link users, problems and optionally contests. Standings are derived from submissions and can be rebuilt from them, which matters when the fast leaderboard store fails.

## API

```http
GET /v1/problems?cursor=...&limit=50           -> 200 { "items": [...], "nextCursor": "..." }
GET /v1/problems/{slug}                        -> 200 { statement, examples, limits, languages }

POST /v1/submissions
Idempotency-Key: 6f1c...                       (client-generated, one per Submit click)
{ "problemSlug": "two-sum", "language": "cpp17", "code": "...", "contestId": "c_42" }
-> 202 { "submissionId": "s_901", "status": "queued" }

GET /v1/submissions/s_901
-> 200 { "status": "running", "testsPassed": 12, "testsTotal": 40 }
-> 200 { "status": "done", "verdict": "time_limit_exceeded", "failedTest": 37, "runtimeMs": 2000, "memoryKb": 18432 }

GET /v1/submissions/s_901/events               (Server-Sent Events: queued, running, done)

GET /v1/contests/c_42/leaderboard?offset=0&limit=50
-> 200 { "asOf": "...", "rows": [{ "rank": 1, "user": "...", "solved": 4, "penalty": 5410 }], "me": { "rank": 1873 } }
```

All endpoints except problem reads require an authenticated user. Code size is capped (for example 64 KB). `POST /submissions` is rate-limited per user (say 1 every 5 s during contests) to stop accidental and deliberate floods.

## High-level design

**View problems.** A **problem service** reads statements from a relational database, fronted by a cache and CDN; problems change rarely, so this is a read-scaling non-issue.

**Submit and get results.** The **submission service** validates the request, writes a submission row (`queued`) with the idempotency key, stores the code, and enqueues a job on a durable **queue**. A pool of **judge workers** pulls jobs, fetches the code and the problem's test set (cached locally on the worker), starts one **sandbox**, compiles and runs all tests inside it, and writes the verdict back. The client polls or subscribes to status.

**Contests.** When a contest submission finishes, the worker publishes a verdict event. A **leaderboard service** updates the durable standings table and a **Redis sorted set** that answers rank queries.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C["Client"] --> GW["API gateway (auth, rate limit)"]
    GW --> PSvc["Problem service"]
    PSvc --> DB[("Postgres")]
    GW --> SS["Submission service"]
    SS --> DB
    SS --> Q[["Judge queue"]]
    Q --> W["Judge workers"]
    W --> SB["Sandboxes"]
    W --> TS[("Test data in object storage")]
    W --> DB
    W --> EV[["Verdict events"]]
    EV --> LB["Leaderboard service"]
    LB --> Z[("Redis sorted sets")]
    GW --> LB
```

Walk one submission: the user clicks Submit; the gateway authenticates and rate-limits; the submission service inserts the row with a unique (user, idempotency key) constraint, stores the code and enqueues `s_901`, returning `202` in about 50 ms. A worker leases the job, launches a sandbox, compiles, runs 40 tests, records `accepted` with the maximum runtime and memory, and publishes the verdict event. The client's SSE stream receives `done`; the leaderboard service updates standings.

## Deep dives

### 1. Running untrusted code safely (isolation)

**Problem.** Submitted code may fork-bomb, allocate 50 GB, write until the disk fills, open sockets to exfiltrate test data, or try kernel exploits to escape. Isolation must hold even against a determined attacker.

**Bad: run code as a separate process on the worker host.** One `system("rm -rf /")` or network call ends the discussion.

**Good: containers with tight limits.** Linux namespaces and cgroups give each run its own filesystem view, process tree and resource caps. Configure: no network namespace connectivity (`--network none`), read-only root filesystem with a small size-capped tmpfs for scratch, non-root user, all capabilities dropped, a seccomp profile limiting system calls, cgroup limits on memory, CPU and **process count** (to stop fork bombs), and caps on output size. The weakness: containers share the host kernel, so a kernel vulnerability can still lead to escape.

**Great: a stronger boundary under the container.** Add a second layer for hostile workloads: **gVisor** runs a user-space kernel that intercepts system calls, so user code never talks to the host kernel directly (at some syscall-performance cost), or **Firecracker** microVMs give each sandbox its own lightweight virtual machine with fast boot. Keep test data out of the sandbox except for the specific input being run, run workers in a network segment with no route to internal services, and treat the worker hosts as disposable (rebuilt regularly).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Code["Untrusted submission"] --> Limits["cgroups: CPU, memory, pids, output size"]
    Limits --> NS["Namespaces: no network, read-only rootfs, tmpfs scratch"]
    NS --> Sec["seccomp profile, no capabilities, non-root user"]
    Sec --> Kern["gVisor user-space kernel or Firecracker microVM"]
    Kern --> Host["Isolated worker host, no route to internal services"]
```

Each layer limits a different failure: resource exhaustion, data access, dangerous syscalls, kernel escape and lateral movement. The interview point is defence in depth: no single mechanism is trusted alone.

### 2. Queue, worker pool and batching tests per submission (latency and cost)

**Problem.** Execution is slow, bursty and must not block API threads; and per-test sandboxes waste most of the time on startup.

**Bad: execute synchronously in the API request.** Requests take seconds, threads pile up at contest start, and a crash loses the submission.

**Good: durable queue plus worker pool, one sandbox per test.** Async and resilient, but 40 sandbox starts per submission dominates latency and cost.

**Great: one sandbox per submission, a harness inside it, and a warm pool.** The worker starts a single sandbox, compiles once, then a small trusted harness runs each test as a child process with its own limits, compares output and stops at the first failure (for an accept/reject verdict there is no need to run the rest). Keep a pool of pre-started, clean sandboxes per language so startup is off the critical path; each sandbox is destroyed after one submission so no state leaks between users.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Q as Judge queue
    participant W as Worker
    participant S as Sandbox
    participant DB as Submissions DB
    Q->>W: lease job s_901 (visibility 60s)
    W->>DB: status=running if status=queued
    W->>S: take warm sandbox, copy code
    S->>S: compile once
    loop each test until first failure
        W->>S: run test i with CPU and wall limits
        S-->>W: output, cpu ms, memory
    end
    W->>S: destroy sandbox
    W->>DB: verdict (conditional on lease)
    W->>Q: ack
```

The worker heartbeats its lease during long runs; if it dies, the job reappears and another worker re-judges it from scratch. Because judging is deterministic and the final write is conditional on lease ownership, a duplicate run is harmless.

**Time limits: CPU time vs wall clock.** Measure each test's limit in **CPU time** of the process tree (via cgroup accounting), so a busy host or a noisy neighbour does not turn a correct solution into a TLE. Also enforce a **wall-clock** limit per test (for example 2 × the CPU limit plus 1 s) to kill programs that sleep or block on input, plus an overall wall budget per submission. Pin sandboxes to dedicated cores and avoid oversubscribing CPU on judge hosts so runtimes are reproducible; publish per-language limit multipliers if slower languages get more time.

Real-world note: PrepAlgo itself works this way. Submissions run in a locked-down Docker sandbox on a private executor host, and all tests for a submission are batched into one sandbox run.

### 3. Contest start: surviving the burst

**Problem.** At 0:00 the problem pages are hit by 50,000 users at once, and minutes later submissions spike 15 to 20 times.

- **Pre-scale on schedule:** contests are known in advance, so scale judge workers to the expected peak 15 minutes before start; reactive autoscaling on queue depth handles the remainder.
- **Cache and pre-warm problem pages:** publish statements to the CDN with an embargo (served only after start time) so the page load is an edge hit, not a database stampede.
- **Separate queues by priority:** contest submissions get their own queue and worker pool so a contest burst does not starve, or get starved by, practice traffic.
- **Backpressure, not failure:** if the queue grows, keep accepting (the queue is the buffer), show queue position, and rate-limit per user. Contest time used for scoring is the **submission time**, not the verdict time, so queueing does not penalise anyone.

### 4. Idempotent submissions and status delivery

**Problem.** Users double-click Submit and flaky networks retry `POST`, which must not create two submissions (that would add a contest penalty). And status checks at contest scale can overload the database.

**Idempotency.** The client generates an idempotency key per Submit click. The submission service inserts with a unique constraint on (user, key); a retry finds the existing row and returns the same `submissionId`. Inside the pipeline, at-least-once delivery is handled by the conditional status transitions above.

**Status.** **Polling** (`GET` every 1 s, backing off to 3 s) is the simple default; serve it from a Redis copy of the status row that workers update, so 50,000 reads/s never touch Postgres. **SSE** is better for the interactive case: one connection per waiting user, fed by a pub/sub channel per submission, and it naturally streams progress (`12 of 40 tests passed`). Either way, the database row remains the source of truth, and a client that reconnects simply reads the final state.

### 5. Leaderboard with Redis sorted sets

**Problem.** Show the top 50 and "my rank" for 50,000 users, updated within seconds, under heavy read load.

**Bad: `ORDER BY solved DESC, penalty ASC` on every request.** Correct but scans and sorts the standings table thousands of times per second.

**Good: periodically materialise the sorted standings** into a cache every 30 s. Cheap, but rank lags and "my rank" needs the full list.

**Great: a Redis sorted set per contest, fed from durable standings.** Encode the ICPC-style ordering into one score: `score = solved × 10^8 − penalty_seconds`, so more solves rank higher and lower penalty breaks ties. `ZREVRANGE` returns the top N in O(log n + N), and `ZREVRANK` returns any user's rank in O(log n).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    V[["Verdict events"]] --> LB["Leaderboard service"]
    LB -->|"first accepted per user and problem"| ST[("Postgres standings (source of truth)")]
    LB -->|"ZADD contest score"| Z[("Redis sorted set")]
    R["Leaderboard reads"] --> Z
    ST -.->|"rebuild after failure or at freeze"| Z
```

The leaderboard service updates the standings row in a transaction (only the first accepted submission per user and problem counts; wrong attempts before it add penalty), then writes the new score to Redis. Reads hit Redis only, with the top-50 response cached for a few seconds. If Redis is lost, rebuild the set from standings in seconds. For a scoreboard freeze in the last hour, stop updating the public set while continuing to update standings, then publish the final set at the end.

## What interviewers look for

- **Mid-level:** an async submission pipeline (queue plus workers), containers with resource limits and no network, a clear verdict model, polling for status and a sorted-set leaderboard.
- **Senior:** layered isolation and why containers alone share a kernel, batching tests in one sandbox with CPU-time limits plus wall-clock guards, idempotent submission and lease-based re-judging, contest pre-scaling and status reads that avoid the database.
- **Staff:** treats isolation as a threat model with layered controls and blast-radius limits, makes fairness measurable (dedicated cores, reproducible runtimes, per-language limits), plans capacity per contest calendar, and designs leaderboard correctness (freeze, rejudges after a bad test case, rebuild from source of truth).

## Common mistakes

- Running user code directly on the API or worker host, or in a container with network access.
- One sandbox per test case, multiplying startup cost by the number of tests.
- Time limits measured in wall-clock time only, so verdicts depend on host load.
- Executing submissions synchronously inside the HTTP request.
- No idempotency key, so a double-click becomes a contest penalty.
- Making Redis the only copy of contest standings.

## Self-review checklist

- [ ] Untrusted code is isolated by at least two independent layers, with no network and capped resources.
- [ ] Submissions are durable before `202`, idempotent per Submit click and judged at least once with conditional writes.
- [ ] All tests of a submission share one sandbox; per-test CPU limits and wall-clock guards are defined.
- [ ] The contest burst is handled by pre-scaling, a separate queue and visible queue position.
- [ ] Status reads do not hit the primary database at contest scale.
- [ ] The leaderboard uses a sorted set with an explicit score encoding and can be rebuilt from durable standings.

## Further reading

- [gVisor documentation](https://gvisor.dev/docs/)
- [Firecracker microVMs](https://firecracker-microvm.github.io/)
- [Redis sorted sets](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/sorted-sets/)
keyTakeaways: Isolation is the first requirement: layer cgroups, namespaces with no network, seccomp and a gVisor or microVM boundary, and treat hosts as disposable.
Accept submissions durably and idempotently, then judge asynchronously from a queue with leased, re-runnable jobs and conditional verdict writes.
Run all tests of a submission in one sandbox, limit each test by CPU time and guard with wall-clock limits for fair, fast verdicts.
Contests are scheduled bursts: pre-scale workers, isolate contest queues, cache problem pages and serve status from cache or SSE.
Use a Redis sorted set with an encoded score for ranks, backed by durable standings that can rebuild it.
